---
title: "Inverting basal shear stress"
---

The plastic solve turns a margin, a bed and a basal shear stress $\tau_b$ into an ice sheet.
$\tau_b$ carries essentially all of the freedom of the reconstruction, so the practical
question is the inverse one: which $\tau_b$ makes the reconstruction match the data? This page
describes how the inverse problem is posed, the two parameterizations of $\tau_b$ in the
examples, and how the tiled parameterization automates the hand-tuned shear-stress domains of
ICESHEET (Gowan et al., 2016, 2021). The gradient itself (implicit differentiation of the
converged solve) is described in [Algorithms §7](algorithms.qmd#sec-ad).

## The inverse problem

We minimize an objective on the reconstruction over $\tau_b$. For present-day ice the natural
target is the observed surface, through `surface_misfit`:

$$
\min_{\tau_b}\; \big\langle\, (z_s(\tau_b) - z_s^{\text{obs}})^2 \,\big\rangle_{\text{mask}},
\qquad z_s(\tau_b) = z_b + H(\tau_b).
$$

`differentiable_thickness` gives the gradient by reverse-mode AD, and the examples minimize the
misfit with Adam. The grounded `mask` is the prescribed margin, an input of ICESHEET that is not
inverted. The recovered ice extent therefore always equals the mask, and only the geometry
inside it is fit.

The number of free parameters in $\tau_b$ should match what the target data can resolve. A
dense present-day surface constrains a dense field, while a sparse paleo target (relative sea
level) constrains only a few regional values. The two parameterizations below sit at these two
ends.

## Two parameterizations

The example
[`examples/invert_taub_greenland.jl`](https://github.com/fesmc/PlasticIceSheet.jl/blob/main/examples/invert_taub_greenland.jl)
implements both and switches between them with the environment variable `METHOD`:

```bash
julia --project=examples examples/invert_taub_greenland.jl                  # METHOD=tiled (default)
METHOD=percell julia --project=examples examples/invert_taub_greenland.jl   # per cell
```

The objective, the Adam loop and the outputs are shared. Only the map from the optimization
parameters to the $\tau_b$ field differs. All results below are for Greenland at 32 km
(GRL-32KM, about 2000 ice cells), `mode = :surface` and `margin = :face`.

### Per cell (`METHOD=percell`)

A full per-cell $\tau_b$ field is regularized to a length scale `REG_KM` by a Gaussian-blur
reparameterization. We optimize a raw field $\varphi$ and set

$$
\tau_b = \operatorname{clamp}\big(K_x\,\varphi\,K_y\big),
$$

where $K_x$ and $K_y$ are separable 1-D Gaussian smoothers with
$\sigma = \texttt{REG\_KM}/\Delta x$ cells. The blur is linear, so it differentiates cleanly
under Zygote, and it ensures that $\tau_b$ varies only on scales of at least `REG_KM`
regardless of the data fit. This parameterization has many effective degrees of freedom and
fits a dense observed surface closely (about 44 m rmse with `REG_KM` = 32 km).

### Tiled (`METHOD=tiled`, default)

The tiled parameterization is low-dimensional and transferable to paleo ice sheets. Cells are
grouped into tiles defined **only from data available for an unknown ice sheet**: bed
roughness (the windowed standard deviation of $z_b$, binned into `N_ROUGH` quantile classes)
crossed with a sediment mask (sediment thickness split into soft and hard at `SED_THRESH`).
The ice thickness and ice-derived drainage basins are never used to draw the tiles. Each tile
$d$ carries one value $\theta_d$:

$$
\tau_b(\mathbf x) = \operatorname{clamp}\Big(\textstyle\sum_d \theta_d\, \mathbb 1[\,\mathbf x \in d\,]\Big),
$$

embedded by a one-hot selector matrix, which is linear and thus differentiable under Zygote.
The default is `N_ROUGH = 4` × 2 sediment classes, i.e., 8 tiles, which reach about 220 m rmse.
The observed surface enters only as the calibration target. This is the modern-surface
calibration Gowan et al. (2021) used for Greenland and Antarctica, and the place a
relative-sea-level objective would take in a paleo reconstruction.

## Relation to ICESHEET

ICESHEET (Gowan et al., 2016) is the same perfectly plastic, equilibrium forward model. In
PaleoMIST (Gowan et al., 2021), $\tau_b$ was chosen by three steps. First, the target was
relative sea level through a GIA model for the paleo ice sheets, plus geological margins, and
the modern surface for Greenland and Antarctica. Second, the shear-stress domains were defined
by topographic variability (mountainous or flat) and refined by surficial geology (continuous
sediment for low $\tau_b$, hard or discontinuous cover for high $\tau_b$). Third, the domain
values were tuned by hand until the fit was acceptable.

The tiled method follows this logic but automates both halves: the domains come from bed
roughness and sediment, and the domain values come from gradient descent. On Greenland it
recovers the premise of Gowan et al.: the soft-sediment tiles settle at about 5–46 kPa and
the hard-bed tiles at about 51–99 kPa.

## How many tiles? A resolution test

The number of domains, which ICESHEET left to judgement, can be chosen quantitatively.
[`examples/invert_taub_sweep_greenland.jl`](https://github.com/fesmc/PlasticIceSheet.jl/blob/main/examples/invert_taub_sweep_greenland.jl)
sweeps the tile count (100 Adam iterations each) and plots the rmse against the number of free
parameters. The knee of that curve is the resolution the data support:

| roughness classes | tiles, roughness only | rmse (m) | tiles, with sediment split | rmse (m) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 319 | 2 | 250 |
| 2 | 2 | 283 | 4 | 237 |
| 3 | 3 | 269 | 6 | 213 |
| 4 | 4 | 273 | 8 | 220 |
| 6 | 6 | 268 | 11 | 212 |
| 8 | 8 | 264 | 15 | 210 |

Sediment controls the fit more than roughness does. A single hard/soft split (2 tiles) reduces
the rmse from about 320 to 250 m, more than eight roughness-only tiles achieve (about 264 m).
The knee lies at about 6 tiles, beyond which further parameters change the rmse by less than
5 m. Even the best tiling (about 210 m) remains well above the per-cell fit (about 44 m).
Thus, a substantial part of the surface signal reflects variations of $\tau_b$ that static bed
roughness and sediment do not explain, most likely the basal thermal and hydrological state.

## Conditioning: choice of mode

The inversions use `mode = :surface`, the default. Its scheme is monotone
([Algorithms §2](algorithms.qmd#sec-surface)), so the residual Jacobian of the adjoint is well conditioned, as for `:flat`.
Including the bed relief, however, improves the fit: with the default 8 tiles `:surface`
reaches about 220 m rmse and `:flat` about 312 m, at a similar cost (about 4–5 min for 250
iterations). `:full` is not suitable, since its damped fixed point does not converge on real
beds, and its dense adjoint system becomes singular on large grids. For finer grids the cost
of the per-cell gradient is dominated by the direct linear solve. See the
`differentiable_thickness` docstring for the iterative-solver option.

## Toward a paleo (RSL) reconstruction

The tiled parameterization links to a paleo reconstruction: keep the bed-derived tiles and
replace the observed-surface objective by relative sea level computed with a GIA model. The
tiles need no knowledge of the ice sheet, so the same setup transfers to an ice sheet whose
geometry is unknown. That is the regime ICESHEET was built for, and the one in which reducing
the number of parameters is required rather than optional.
